newsitem.title: USA: Ahmanson drops bid to acquire Great Western.
newsitem.headline: Ahmanson drops bid to acquire Great Western.

text.p: H.F. Ahmanson & Co. on Wednesday abandoned its $6.7 billion hostile bid to acquire Great Western Financial Corp., clearing the way for Great Western to merge with friendly suitor Washington Mutual Inc.

The move, announced before the market opened, came a day after Ahmanson's request to delay Great Western's special shareholder meeting was rejected by the Delaware Chancery Court. Ahmanson had hoped to postpone the June 13 meeting so it could rally more support for its offer.
Analysts said Tuesday's ruling left Ahmanson few options but to raise its bid, which could dilute returns to its shareholders and leave the banking company open to criticism.

"They were basically a frustrated, hostile bidder whose bid was not worth significantly more (than Washington Mutual's)," said Steven Cohen, partner with Kellner, DiLeo and Co, a New York-based merger and arbitrage firm.
"Courts are not inclined to interfere with merger plans or grant injunctions unless the complaining party has a very substantial claim," Cohen said.
Ahmanson stock jumped $1 to $41.25 on the New York Stock Exchange after the company's announcement on speculation that Ahmanson might now become a takeover target itself.

"The countdown has started to see how much longer Ahmanson can remain independent," said Charlotte Chamberlain, of Jefferies and Co. "My sense is there's just one trophy thrift franchise left in California with market share above 5 percent and it's Home Savings."

Ahmanson, the Irwindale, Calif.-based parent of Home Savings of America, launched its hostile offer for Great Western in February. Great Western, based in Chatsworth, Calif., rejected the bid and subsequently agreed to be acquired by Seattle-based Washington Mutual in a $6.74 billion deal that will create the largest U.S. thrift, with $86 billion in assets.
In a statement issued early Wednesday, Ahmanson Chairman Charles Rinehart said the company concluded it could not win without raising its bid, something Ahamanson had already done once.

"We remain absolutely committed to shareholder value and will continue to exercise discipline in merger efforts as in all other endeavours," Rinehart said. "We still believe that Great Western was an attractive partner, but not at the expense of returns to our shareholders."

Ahmanson's decision to withdraw represented a bitter defeat for the California thrift. For three months, Ahmanson and Washington Mutual bickered over who had the superior offer, appealing to Great Western shareholders in full-page advertisements in major newspapers.
The battle took on a surprisingly personal tone with Great Western accusing Ahmanson of planning to lay off thousands of Great Western employees in order to make the merger work.
Ahmanson argued that because both it and Great Western were located in the same geographic area, it could wring more expense reductions from a combination.
But Washington Mutual cited its record of more than 20 successful acquisitions in the past 10 years and said it could cut expenses and grow revenue at the same time.
Rinehart said Ahmanson will pursue its strategy to grow as a full-service bank for consumers and small business.
Great Western rose 62.5 cents to $48 on the NYSE while Washington Mutual added 25 cents to $54 on Nasdaq.
